Whoredoms
hōr'dumz
n. pl. (acts of harlotry; figuratively, covenant unfaithfulness; rendering Hebrew zenunim)
From whore, Saxon hore, with the ending -dom denoting condition or state, as in freedom and kingdom. Hebrew zenunim is a plural of intensity from zanah, to commit fornication, and in the prophets it is applied to Israel's idolatry far more often than to literal immorality.

Biblical Definition

Whoredoms is the prophets' word for idolatry, and the choice of vocabulary is itself the doctrine: because the covenant is a marriage, its breach is adultery rather than mere disobedience. God commands Hosea to enact it: “Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD” (Hosea 1:2) — a prophet's marriage made into a living sermon, so that Israel could see what she looked like. Jeremiah presses the charge over the whole landscape: “Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with… and thou hast polluted the land with thy whoredoms and with thy wickedness” (Jeremiah 3:2). Hosea names the mechanism, which is not appetite but a settled disposition: “the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err, and they have gone a whoring from under their God” (Hosea 4:12). And the word attaches to a name that became a byword when Jehu answered Joram, asking what peace there could be “so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many?” (2 Kings 9:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

Acts of harlotry, and in the prophets the standing figure for idolatry — because the covenant is a marriage, breaking it is adultery. Hosea was commanded to enact the charge in his own household.

WHOREDOMS, n. plural of whoredom. [from whore, Sax. hore, with the termination -dom, state or condition.] Lewdness; fornication; practice of unlawful commerce with the other sex.

2. In Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the true God for false gods.

3. Unfaithfulness to a covenant, viewed as marital treachery.

4. As in Hosea; the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord, Hos. 1.

5. The whoredoms of Jezebel and her witchcrafts, 2 Kings 9.

Key Scripture

Hosea 1:2 — "The beginning of the word of the LORD by Hosea. And the LORD said to Hosea, Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD."

Hosea 4:12 — "My people ask counsel at their stocks, and their staff declareth unto them: for the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err, and they have gone a whoring from under their God."

2 Kings 9:22 — "And it came to pass, when Joram saw Jehu, that he said, Is it peace, Jehu? And he answered, What peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many?"

Jeremiah 3:2 — "Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with. In the ways hast thou sat for them, as the Arabian in the wilderness; and thou hast polluted the land with thy whoredoms and with thy wickedness."

Modern Corruption

Idolatry is imagined as a foreign and antique problem, and the marital language of the prophets is thought excessive. Scripture chooses that language deliberately, because the covenant is a marriage and its breach is betrayal rather than mere rule-breaking.

expand to see more

The instinct to soften this vocabulary misses why God chose it. Had Israel's sin been merely the breaking of rules, the language of trespass would have sufficed; the prophets reach for the language of a betrayed husband because the relationship is a marriage covenant, and the wound is personal. Hosea is the extreme case: God does not only say it, he makes his prophet live it, so that Israel watching Hosea buy back his wife would see what God was doing with her. To flinch from the word is to lose the tenderness underneath it, since the same book says I will betroth thee unto me for ever.

The principle to recover is that idolatry is perennial and domestic. John ends his epistle with little children, keep yourselves from idols, written to Christians, not to pagans; and Paul says covetousness is idolatry. Hosea 4:12 identifies the trouble as a spirit of whoredoms, a settled bent rather than an isolated lapse, which is why the remedy in Scripture is never mere resolution but a new heart. And 2 Kings 9:22 answers the question every compromising generation asks — is it peace? — with the only honest reply: what peace, so long as the whoredoms are so many?

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zenunim is whoredoms, a plural of intensity from zanah, to play the harlot; taznuth is the same idea. Greek porneia renders it, giving English pornography, and is used of spiritual as well as bodily fornication.

expand to see more

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit fornication, to go a whoring; used of Israel after other gods.

Hebrew zenunim (H2183) — whoredoms; the intensive plural of Hosea 1:2.

Hebrew taznuth (H8457) — harlotry, whoredom; Ezekiel's term in his indictment of Jerusalem.

Hebrew naaph (H5003) — to commit adultery; the covenant breach stated in marital terms.

Greek porneia (G4202) — fornication; used of Babylon's spiritual harlotry in Revelation.

Usage

"Of the charge enacted in a prophet's household: the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD (Hosea 1:2)."

"Of a settled disposition rather than a lapse: the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err (Hosea 4:12)."

"Of the impossibility of peace with them: so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel… are so many (2 Kings 9:22)."
